title: Solar panels and dynamic contracts: a good or bad combination?
excerpt: Solar panels and dynamic contracts: is this a good or bad combination? In this blog, we dive into the details!
contentHtml:
Dynamic energy contracts are all the rage. More and more often, you hear that a dynamic contract is very advantageous in combination with solar panels. Here are some examples: AD, Duurzamerhand, and Solar365. But solar energy is fed back into the grid by everyone at the same time (in the middle of the day), and that’s when you’d expect the dynamic prices for feed-in to be lowest/most unfavorable, right? And why would solar panel owners be able to get more net metering benefits compared to a fixed energy contract? We looked into it!

How exactly do net metering and feed-in tariffs work with the different contracts?

Until 2027, households can still benefit from the net metering scheme, whereby the (solar) energy fed back into the grid is offset against the energy consumed. However, depending on the type of energy contract, there are significant differences in how net metering works.

Offsetting with a fixed contract

With a fixed contract, you can deduct the electricity you feed back into the grid from your total consumption on an annual basis. (Variable contracts work in the same way, except that the fixed rates can be adjusted during the year. A variable contract is therefore not a dynamic contract – do you understand?!). Back to netting: if your annual consumption exceeds your feed-in, you do not pay the fixed energy rate on your total consumption, but on your net netted consumption (total consumption minus feed-in). If you feed in more than you have consumed, you will receive a feed-in tariff for this surplus. The feed-in tariff is almost always (much) lower than the rate you pay for the electricity you purchase.

In addition, there are the feed-in costs, the extra costs for feeding electricity back into the grid, which are currently charged by almost all suppliers. The exact feed-in costs vary per supplier. But please note: these feed-in costs are not offset, so they are calculated for every kWh fed back into the grid. For a number of suppliers, the feed-in costs are even higher than the feed-in tariff. This means that you may end up paying for the electricity you feed back into the grid instead of receiving money for it!

Calculation example: offsetting with a fixed contract

Suppose you have an average three-person household and consume 3,000 kWh per year, while generating 4,500 kWh with 16 solar panels. Your own consumption is around 25%, so you take 2,200 kWh from the grid and feed 3,700 kWh back into it. This is a net feed-in, so you pay an average electricity rate of €0.32 per kWh for 0 kWh.

Consumptions: 0 kWh × €0.32 = €0

Because more energy is fed back than consumed, you will receive a feed-in tariff for the net surplus of 1500 kWh. The average feed-in tariff is €0.10 per kWh.

Feed-in tariff: 1500 kWh × €0.10 = €150

However, there are also feed-in costs for the total energy fed back into the grid without netting. On average, the feed-in costs are €0.13 per kWh, so:

Feed-in costs: 3,700 kWh × €0.13 = €481

Total annual costs: €0 + €481 – €150 = €331

Net metering with a dynamic contract

With a dynamic contract, netting works slightly differently. (Yep, even more complicated!) Instead of netting on an annual basis, netting is done on an hourly basis.

For the energy you draw from the grid, you pay the purchase price for that specific hour. The purchase price consists of the market price, purchase fee, energy tax, and VAT. If you draw energy from the grid between 2:00 p.m. and 3:00 p.m., this will be charged at the purchase price between 2:00 p.m. and 3:00 p.m. You also receive the feed-in tariff on an hourly basis, which consists only of the exchange price and purchase fee. This means you do not get the energy tax back!

With a fixed contract, there are feed-in costs because the supplier pays you more for your feed-in energy than the current market price, and this difference is therefore offset by the feed-in costs. With dynamic contracts, this is not necessary: you receive exactly the market price and there are no ‘hidden costs’ for that feed-in. With a dynamic contract, you therefore have no additional feed-in costs, as these are already included in the market price.

Calculation example: netting with a dynamic contract

Let’s use the same values as in the previous calculation example: consumption of 3000 kWh and total generation of 4500 kWh. Your total grid consumption is again 2200 kWh and you feed back 3700 kWh. Your grid consumption is charged at the market price, including purchase compensation, energy tax, and VAT for the hours during which you use the energy. This price varies per hour, but for convenience, we will assume that the average dynamic price is €0.22 per kWh:

Consumption costs: 2200 kWh × €0.22 = €484

For the energy you generate and feed back into the grid, you will receive compensation based on the market price, including purchase compensation, for the hours during which you fed energy back into the grid. Suppose the average feed-in tariff is €0.07 per kWh:

Feed-in tariff: 3700 kWh × €0.07 = €259

Total annual costs: €484 – €259 = €225

The difference between the purchase price and the sales fee you receive from your energy supplier is the energy tax, which amounts to approximately €0.13 per kWh.

The comparison: how advantageous is netting with a fixed or dynamic contract?

Now that net metering has been explained, the question remains: how do the two compare? The tables below provide an overview of the total electricity costs for fixed contracts versus dynamic contracts:

1. More generated than consumed

2. More consumption than generation

Based on the tables above, it appears that dynamic rates are cheaper than fixed rates in both scenarios. The feed-in costs of fixed contracts play a huge role in this!

When more energy is generated than consumed on an annual basis, a dynamic contract therefore yields considerable savings, because there are no feed-in costs but rather a feed-in tariff. However, in a situation where consumption exceeds generation, the cost advantage of dynamic contracts is less significant.

How smart is a dynamic contract for households with solar panels?

Here is the most important and simplest conclusion: a dynamic contract is particularly beneficial if you can also consume dynamically! Solar panel owners can significantly optimize their savings with a dynamic contract by managing their energy consumption wisely. Because prices fluctuate hourly, a dynamic contract offers the opportunity to take advantage of cheaper energy at specific times and avoid the costs of expensive energy.

Hourly price differences: In general, prices are lower in the afternoon than in the morning and evening. In the afternoon, there is a lot of (cheap) solar energy available, which results in low prices. Many households with solar panels also feed energy back into the grid during these hours and receive this lower price for doing so. In contrast, energy is often purchased at higher prices in the morning and evening.

Smart shifting of consumption: By turning on your dishwasher or washing machine in the afternoon instead of in the evening, for example, you can take advantage of lower prices. This reduces expensive energy consumption and cheap feed-in of solar energy. Below you can see how smart shifting of your energy consumption works and how you can save money with it.

Let’s take a step-by-step look, based on one sunny day!

The graph shows the dynamic stock market price (including purchase price) over the course of the day.

It is clear to see that prices are lowest during the afternoon. Most solar power is generated during these hours, so supply is high while demand is relatively low in the afternoon, resulting in low prices.

The consumption pattern of a household has been added to this.

The trend is clear: the expensive hours coincide with peak consumption. The cheap hours are when consumption is low: market forces at work!

The green line shows the generation of solar energy throughout the day.

Here you can clearly see how the high level of solar power generation ensures low prices.

Normal consumption: The light green area shows the total feed-in, while the light red area shows the total consumption from the grid.

It is immediately apparent that during peak times of the day (7:00 a.m. and 7:00 p.m.), a lot of power is being drawn from the grid.

Smart consumption: This graph shows a situation in which consumption has been shifted in a smart way. Energy consumption during peak hours (7:00 a.m. and 7:00 p.m.) has been shifted to the afternoon. This has an impact on feed-in, but also results in less (expensive) grid consumption. The cost savings are detailed in the table below. Please note: this is only an example of one sunny day.

Then in numbers:

The following table shows the total picture of consumption, generation, grid consumption, and feed-in for a single day. Smart consumption means less is taken from the grid and less is fed back in, with both decreasing by the same amount. However, the costs for grid consumption are higher than the compensation for feed-in, which will result in the savings shown in the second table below.

The values in the table below for a fixed contract are based on the following averages: Energy rate (0.32 €/kWh), feed-in costs (0.13 €/kWh), and feed-in tariff (0.10 €/kWh). The values for a dynamic contract are based on market prices and energy tax (0.13 €/kWh). Network management costs and standing charges are not included in this calculation example, as it is based on the costs for a single day.

Please note: because dynamic rates are dynamic (duh), the above table can vary greatly from day to day!

Based on this calculation example of this “standard sunny day”:

  • Due to the net metering scheme, fixed contracts are slightly cheaper than dynamic contracts on this day.
  • Smarter energy consumption reduces feed-in costs for fixed contracts. For dynamic contracts, it results in lower feed-in tariffs but also lower consumption costs.
  • With a dynamic contract, you can save more money than with a fixed contract by consuming smartly—you can almost halve your costs!

The conclusion: dynamic contracts are smart for dynamic users!

Until 2027, fixed-term contracts may be more advantageous if:

  1. You make good use of the net metering scheme (if your annual consumption can be almost completely offset), and your supplier does not charge excessively high feed-in costs.
  2. Your energy consumption follows the average pattern: your consumption mainly occurs in the morning and evening, and you have few devices that you control flexibly.

Dynamic energy contracts offer solar panel owners more transparency than fixed contracts, and become really interesting when energy consumption can also be dynamic. In other words, as soon as consumers can smartly take advantage of low hourly prices and higher feed-in tariffs.

How can you do this? By increasing your own use of solar energy! There are a few ways to do this:

  1. Home battery – This allows you to store the solar power you generate and use it later instead of power from the grid. Sounds ideal, but the purchase costs are quite high.
  2. Charging an electric car using solar power – This is a smart solution, but the car is not always parked outside when you have surplus energy available.
  3. Smart control of appliances – Think about timing your washing machine or dishwasher when the sun is shining. This helps in any case, but the savings are often not that great and it requires active control on a daily basis.

That’s all well and good, but in practice, many people encounter the same problems: these solutions are expensive, require changes in behavior, or are simply not always usable. Fortunately, there is an alternative that is affordable, efficient, and simple: the WaterAccu. This smart system helps you make the most of solar energy, without any hassle.
